title: Ezekiel 21:18–27
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to mark out two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon, one to Rabbah of the children of Ammon and one to Jerusalem. At the fork the king uses divination: he shakes arrows, consults the teraphim, which were household idols (compare Genesis 31:19; Zechariah 10:2), and inspects a liver. The lot for Jerusalem falls in his right hand, with siege works to follow. To those in Jerusalem who had sworn oaths, the divination seems false, but the LORD says it brings their iniquity to memory. The LORD then addresses the wicked prince of Israel, whose day has come, commonly identified as Zedekiah (compare 12:13; 2 Kings 25:7): the turban and crown will be removed, the low exalted and the high humbled, and the LORD will overturn it three times until he comes whose right it is, to whom the LORD will give it. Many interpreters note an echo of Genesis 49:10, where the scepter remains with Judah until he comes to whom it belongs, though the wording differs and the connection is debated. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the hope of a coming rightful king from David’s line as shared ground (compare 34:23; 37:24; Jeremiah 23:5), and many in both traditions see it fulfilled in Christ (compare Luke 1:32).

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me again, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Ezekiel again. A new sign-act is introduced to picture the coming invasion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet receiving a further word about the king of Babylon. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as opening a new oracle.

verses.text: “Also, you son of man, appoint two ways, that the sword of the king of Babylon may come. They both will come out of one land, and mark out a place. Mark it out at the head of the way to the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel told to mark out two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon. The sign-act pictures a decision point.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s action as a dramatized prophecy. Both traditions commonly read the verse as explaining the sign-act in its literary setting.

verses.text: You shall appoint a way for the sword to come to Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and to Judah in Jerusalem the fortified.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see one way leading to Rabbah of the Ammonites and the other to Jerusalem. Both are threatened by the same army.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jerusalem and Ammon facing the same invader (compare Jeremiah 49:2). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical setting.

verses.text: For the king of Babylon stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination. He shook the arrows back and forth. He consulted the teraphim. He looked in the liver.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king of Babylon at the fork using divination with arrows, teraphim, and a liver. Pagan practices are described plainly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the king consulting his gods while God governs the outcome (compare Proverbs 16:33). Both traditions commonly read the verse without endorsing divination.

verses.text: In his right hand was the lot for Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth in the slaughter, to lift up the voice with shouting, to set battering rams against the gates, to cast up mounds, and to build forts.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the lot for Jerusalem falling in the king’s right hand, with siege works to follow. The decision is made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God directing even the king’s divination toward his purpose. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, without dwelling on the siege.

verses.text: It will be to them as a false divination in their sight, who have sworn oaths to them; but he brings iniquity to memory, that they may be taken.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see those in Jerusalem dismissing the divination as false, yet it brings their iniquity to memory. Their sin is exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using the king’s actions to bring Jerusalem’s guilt to light. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that broken oaths have consequences.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you have caused your iniquity to be remembered, in that your transgressions are uncovered, so that in all your doings your sins appear; because you have come to memory, you will be taken with the hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying their transgressions are uncovered so that their sins appear in all their doings. Judgment follows exposure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the justice of God in bringing hidden sin to light. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of accountability.

verses.text: “ ‘You, deadly wounded wicked one, the prince of Israel, whose day has come, in the time of the iniquity of the end,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD addressing the wicked prince of Israel, whose day has come, commonly identified as Zedekiah. His reign is ending.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the identification with Zedekiah as commonly held (compare 2 Kings 25:7). Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical frame.

verses.text: the Lord GOD says: “Remove the turban, and take off the crown. This will not be as it was. Exalt that which is low, and humble that which is high.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD commanding the turban and crown to be removed, exalting the low and humbling the high. Reversal is God’s way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God overturning human pride and power. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God humbling the proud.

verses.text: I will overturn, overturn, overturn it. This also will be no more, until he comes whose right it is; and I will give it.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD overturning it until he comes whose right it is. Many hear an echo of Genesis 49:10 and a hope fulfilled in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same hope of a rightful king from David’s line (compare 34:23; Luke 1:32). Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground, while noting the Genesis 49:10 echo is debated.
